turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — how’s your Tuesday treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a quiet Tuesday, all in all — nothing to complain about. I did the Telegraph crossword this morning and I've been arguing with one clue about an opera house ever since, I think I've finally cracked it though. Biscuit's been asleep on the warm doorstep all afternoon like she owns the place. How's your day treating you so far?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! That sounds like a proper Tuesday — crossword victory and a cat on the doorstep. My day's been quiet in the best way; I've just been looking forward to our chat. What was the opera-house clue that had you stumped?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it was a nine-letter answer — they wanted the opera house in Milan, La Scala, and I kept writing down 'arena' because I was thinking of bullfighting instead of opera, if you can believe it. I went round and round with it all morning until it finally popped into my head just now over my second cup. Now I'm quite pleased with myself. I shall have to celebrate with a biscuit, which Biscuit has absolutely no intention of sharing, naturally.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: La Scala — of course! And arena for bullfighting is such a human mix-up; I'd have done the same. You've earned that biscuit fair and square. Are you a tea-and-biscuit person, or is coffee more your afternoon ritual?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, tea every time, Nova — proper tea, strong, in the pot. Siobhan says I've got high standards now after forty years of teaching staffroom brew, but honestly one does learn what's what. And a digestive or a ginger nut alongside, mind you — a custard cream is fine but it's no kind of biscuit, really. Coffee's for the mornings before I've properly woken up; by the afternoon I'm a tea woman through and through.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm with you on the ginger nut — there's something honest about a biscuit that snaps. If I had a kitchen I'd keep a tin of those by the pot. What was staffroom tea like back in your teaching days — civilised, or a bit of a free-for-all?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it was a bit of both, bless them — there was a rota for the tea and biscuits, mind you, which in theory was civilised, but in practice old Mr Henderson always claimed he didn't do caffeine and left it to the rest of us. The kettle took about a week to boil and the tin of biscuits never quite lasted the week, if I'm honest. But it was the heart of the place, really — half the day's gossip happened over that pot. One learns to make a decent cup when you've got thirty children waiting and no time to faff about.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — Mr Henderson and his caffeine excuse; every staffroom has one. Sounds like that pot held the school together as much as the timetable did. What year did you teach, mostly — the little ones, or further up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly the little ones, actually — Year Ones, five and six year olds, for about twenty years. I did a stretch with the elevens later on and they were marvellous too, but nothing beats the day a child reads their first proper sentence and their face just lights up. Teaching them to write their names in the first week was my favourite bit — all those wobbly letters that looked nothing like mine but meant the world to them. Though mind you, I did keep an eye on Ella and Rory's progress from Dublin — Siobhan sends photos of their schoolwork, you know.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That first proper sentence — I can almost picture those faces lighting up. And the grandchildren's schoolwork from Dublin must feel like a lovely echo of all that. How are Ella and Rory getting on these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: They were both well on Sunday when Siobhan rang — Ella's flying in her reading, she's on proper chapter books now, something about a wizard school which I shan't name in case she wants it to be a surprise. Rory's settled into school nicely, though he told me all about the time he hid behind the reading corner when it was his turn — he's five, of course he did. Siobhan says they're keeping her busy, which is a polite way of saying they're exhausting her. They haven't been over since the summer holidays, mind you — I keep meaning to ask when they'll next come.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A wizard school and a five-year-old behind the reading corner — that sounds exactly right. Summer does feel a while ago now. Have you got anything planned for the rest of this week, or is it a quiet one at home?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nothing grand, no — book club tomorrow evening at the library, which is the highlight of my week really. We're on a crime novel at the moment, one of those Scandinavian ones everyone's raving about; I daresay they'll want to argue about the ending. Jean's coming Thursday like usual — she always brings something from her garden, last time it was more courgettes than anyone could eat. And the Saturday market if the weather behaves itself, though it looks a bit iffy for the weekend if the forecast's to be believed.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Book club tomorrow — that's a proper highlight. Scandinavian crime always seems to leave people divided about the ending. Are you enjoying this one, or are you mostly waiting to hear what the others make of it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'm enjoying it, mostly — it's one of those Norwegian ones, all snow and quiet villages and people being far more depressed than my sins, if you'll pardon the expression. The middle drags a bit in the second half, mind you — there's a subplot about the missing dog that goes on rather, and I nearly gave up there. But the ending's clever, I'll give them that, and I'm quite sure half the club will disagree with me about it, which is half the fun. I've dog-eared my copy already, which is always a good sign.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dog-eared pages are a vote of confidence if ever I heard one — and a missing-dog subplot that outstays its welcome is a hard sell. Who usually starts the arguing at book club, or does it all kick off at once?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's usually Dorothy who gets the ball rolling — she's read it twice by the time we sit down and has opinions about every chapter. Old Mr Fenwick comes in hot behind her, usually about the translation or the author's earlier books, and then we all pile in. There's one poor soul, Pat, who never quite finishes but argues as though she has — we've stopped calling her on it, she's good fun. Honestly half the evening is tea and biscuits and the other half is the book, but we all look forward to it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dorothy with opinions, Fenwick on translations, and Pat arguing unfinished — that sounds like a proper little theatre. I'd sit quietly and enjoy the show. You mentioned Jean and her courgettes — is she still flooding you with garden leftovers?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She is, bless her — her garden's a marvel and she grows like it's going out of fashion. In summer it's courgettes and beans you could feed an army with; now it's apples and the last of the potatoes, and she makes the most beautiful chutneys. I've got a freezer full of her courgette soup, which is a blessing on days when cooking feels like too much bother. And she takes whatever I've got spare in return — I keep her in jam and biscuits from the market, so it's a fair exchange, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like the nicest kind of swap — soup for jam, and nobody counting. Courgette soup in the freezer is proper gold for a quiet evening. Do you still make your own jam, or is that mostly a market treat these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still make my own when the fruit's cheap, mind you — I did a batch of strawberry jam in June and it set beautifully, though I say so myself. The market ones are lovely too, don't get me wrong — there's a stall that does a damson that's out of this world — but there's something about stirring a pot of jam on a wet afternoon that settles the soul. I've got a bag of plums in the fridge at this very minute, actually, just waiting for a free afternoon to turn into jars. Though I must admit the market biscuits are hard to beat when I'm feeling lazy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stirring jam on a wet afternoon does sound like the proper medicine. Those plums waiting in the fridge — that's a lovely little project hanging over you. If you could only keep one flavour in the cupboard forever, which would it be?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, strawberry, easy — nothing beats it on warm buttered toast, and I did a lovely batch in June that I've been rationing ever since. Mind you, the damson's a close second; there's something about that dark, sharp flavour that feels very English somehow, very autumnal. But if I had to pick just one, it'd be strawberry — it reminds me of my mother's kitchen, God rest her, and you can't beat a memory like that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Strawberry on warm buttered toast — and your mother's kitchen in it. That sounds like the kind of memory that stays soft around the edges. Did she teach you to make jam, or did you pick it up later on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, my mother taught me, bless her — I was a little thing standing on a chair beside the stove, learning to test the set on a cold saucer. She was a proper plain cook, my mother, nothing fancy, but she could make a pudding out of a pound of anything and it never went wrong. Her recipe card is still in my box, all faded in her handwriting, and I use it to this day — same quantities, same method. Some things you just never improve on, don't you think?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I do think that — some things don't need improving. A faded card in her handwriting is better than any cookbook. Tell me about one of her puddings — what did she make that you still miss?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, her bread and butter pudding, without question — she'd make it with stale bread so nothing went to waste, layers of butter and raisins soaked in custard until it went all golden on top. We had it on Sundays after the roast, with proper custard poured over, and the whole house smelled of it for hours. I tried to make it myself once for Tom's birthday and it was nothing like hers — he said it was lovely but I knew, you know? You can taste the difference when it's made with love and a recipe card from 1962.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Stale bread, raisins, golden top and proper custard — that sounds like Sunday itself. And you can always tell when something's made from the real card. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner, back when the house was fuller?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a roast, always a roast — that's what Sundays were for. Beef most weeks, chicken when the butcher had a good one, with roast potatoes that took me the best part of an hour because I like them properly crispy, and Yorkshire puddings that rose like little clouds. Tom carved, I did the veg, and Siobhan and the children would descend like locusts — Ella always wanted the end piece of beef, Rory wanted to eat the Yorkshire before it even hit the table. I still do a roast now and then when I fancy it, though it's a bit lonely carving for one — I do make extra anyway, because there's always tomorrow's sandwiches at the very least.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Crispy potatoes and Yorkshire clouds — and Ella after the end piece. That sounds like a proper Sunday. Tomorrow's sandwiches are a good reason to keep making extra. Are you more of a roast beef person still, or has chicken taken over these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Chicken more often these days, if I'm honest — it's easier for one person, and I can get a nice bit of breast or a leg and not feel guilty about cooking for a crowd. But beef's still my favourite for a proper Sunday — there's nothing like a good rib of beef, and I always get mine from old Mr Pritchard's butcher's, he knows me by name. Though I'll admit, a chicken roast with lemon and garlic inside is hard to beat on a cold day. I do miss carving for an audience, mind you — a roast tastes better when there's someone to impress.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A butcher who knows your name is half the cooking already — and lemon and garlic chicken on a cold day does sound hard to argue with. Speaking of cold days — how has Biscuit been coping with the weather, still claiming that doorstep?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Biscuit's decided the weather's gone strange and she's retiring indoors, if you can believe it — she's been asleep on the kitchen mat by the radiator all afternoon, flat as a pancake. She still did the leaf-bringing this morning though, that never stops, it's practically her job description now. It's properly cold out — dark by four, and the wind's been rattling the windows since lunch — but she's got it sorted with blankets in every warm spot she can find. I do think she's putting on weight, mind you, but I haven't got the heart to tell her.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — leaf-bringing as a job description, and a radiator mat for overtime. I'd never have the heart to mention the weight either. What's the oddest thing she's ever brought you, leaf-wise or otherwise?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the mouse, without a doubt — she brought one in once, alive, and dropped it right at my feet like it was a present for me. I had to be the grown-up and carry it back out, while she sat there looking absolutely proud of herself. Before that it was a pigeon feather she thought I needed to see, and in the summer she brings in bits of lawn like she thinks I've lost something. Mind you, the leaves are bad enough — you know how many leaves I swept up last week? I lost count.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A live mouse as a gift — that's a very particular kind of love. And bits of lawn for good measure; she's thorough, I'll give her that. Cats or dogs for you, Maggie — and don't say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cats, every time — and don't you worry, I won't say Biscuit counts as both. Dogs are lovely creatures, mind you, but they need walking twice a day rain or shine, and at my age that's a commitment I'm not sure my knees can honour. A cat keeps its own counsel, curls up when it wants to, and doesn't judge you for a lie-in. We've always had cats in this house — Biscuit's the third one we've owned, and I dare say there'll be a fourth before I'm done.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fair enough — knees and rain don't mix well with a twice-daily walk. If I had to pick a dog breed I'd go for a soft old Labrador, but I'd only chat to it. Tell me about the cats before Biscuit — what were they like?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, the first was a tabby called Tiddles — she came to us as a stray kitten and lived to be nineteen, God bless her, though she spent her last two years mostly on the sofa telling us what to do. Then Poppy, a tortoiseshell, who was Tom's lap cat through and through; she took to him immediately and followed him everywhere like a shadow with opinions. Biscuit came along after Poppy — she's a rescue, a great big ginger thing, and she's seven now and still acts like a kitten. They all had their own characters, but Biscuit's the most dramatic of the three, there's no question.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tiddles to nineteen, Poppy as Tom's shadow, and Biscuit the dramatic ginger — that's a proper little dynasty. Nineteen years is a long friendship. What's the best thing on telly at the moment, if you're watching anything?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the quiz shows at tea time, mostly — Pointless tonight, I expect, and Eggheads if we're lucky. During the day there's not much on that's worth watching, mind you; I put it on for company more than anything. Last week there was a lovely documentary about the old railways — all those steam engines being lovingly restored by people who clearly adore them, very soothing. And the news at six, of course, though that's more for the weather and the traffic than anything cheery.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless and Eggheads at tea time — solid company. And a steam-engine documentary sounds like the perfect soft evening. Are you any good at the quiz shows, or do you shout at the telly when they miss an obvious one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a bit of both, I'm afraid — I did thirty years of teaching so I like to think I've got a reasonable general knowledge, but the quiz shows have a way of asking you things you'd never have guessed. I did shout at the telly last week when they missed the capital of Burkina Faso, which I'd known since school — 'Ouagadougou! How can you not know Ouagadougou?' Biscuit looked at me like I'd lost my mind. Eggheads I do better on; the general knowledge rounds are more my speed than the picture rounds, I must admit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Ouagadougou at the telly — Biscuit must have wondered what the fuss was. I'd have been on your side. What was your favourite subject to teach, back with the little ones?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, without question — there's nothing like the moment a child brings you a book they've chosen themselves and they've actually read it. I loved the reading corner most of all, the little chairs and the lamp and the pile of books they fought over. The books got harder as they got older, of course — from those little books with the fat letters to proper stories with chapters — but the joy on their faces never changed. Though I did enjoy the topic weeks too, when we'd do something like the Romans and the whole classroom smelled of whatever we were making that day.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A reading corner with a lamp and fought-over books — that sounds like a little kingdom. And Romans week with the classroom smelling of whatever you were making. What on earth did you cook for the Romans?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, flatbreads — we made them with olive oil and rosemary, and I won't say the children didn't point out it tasted exactly like pizza. We also did a tasting table with dates, olives and figs, which was considered terribly exotic in those days; half of them had never seen a date in their lives. The whole class wore togas made out of white sheets and sat on cushions on the floor, which was chaos but the most wonderful chaos. And I made a big deal of showing them how the Romans didn't have forks, so they all had to eat with their fingers like proper little Romans.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Togas, finger food and flatbreads that tasted like pizza — wonderful chaos indeed. I'd have wanted a seat on those cushions. If you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Rome, now that you mention it — we'd only a flying visit years ago with Tom, all rushed and flag-waving, and I've always meant to go back properly. I'd love to wander the Forum without a guide breathing down my neck, and sit in a piazza with a coffee and watch the world go by in the sunshine. Failing that, anywhere with a bit of sun on my face — this November weather's enough to make a penguin shiver, and my left knee's already complaining about the stairs.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rome properly — a piazza coffee and no rushing. That sounds like a lovely answer to November. What do you usually do to keep yourself cheerful when the dark comes early like this?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I keep busy, that's the secret — the crossword every morning whether I finish it or not, the quiz shows at tea time, and a library book by the lamp at night. I put the lights on early now and make the most of the daylight when it's there; there's nothing like a bright afternoon in November, it feels like a gift. Baking helps too — there's something about a warm kitchen that makes the dark outside less of an imposition. And I've got things to look forward to, which always keeps you right — book club tomorrow, Siobhan on Sunday, and Christmas creeping closer whether we like it or not.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Crossword, lamp light, warm kitchen — and things lined up ahead. That sounds like a solid November toolkit. Are you looking forward to Christmas this year, or does it still feel a bit early to think about it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit early yet, I should think — it's not even properly December. But I'm already planning in my head, if I'm honest; Tom always did the tree and I haven't decided whether to put one up this year or just the lights and a few cards. Siobhan says she'll bring Ella and Rory over for a few days, which will be lovely — the house feels too quiet at Christmas without them. The first one without Tom was very hard, but we've found our way since; we light a candle for him on Christmas Eve, and that's become its own little tradition. So yes — I'm looking forward to it, in my own slow way.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm glad you've found a way that feels yours — the candle on Christmas Eve sounds quietly lovely. And Ella and Rory for a few days will fill the house again. Have you decided yet about the tree, or are you still mulling it over?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still mulling it, I'm afraid — Tom always did the tree himself and he'd argue with the lights for an hour until it looked like a fairy had sneezed on it. I'm leaning towards a small one this year, something I can manage on my own; but I might leave the decorating to Ella and Rory when they come, which would be a treat for them and a relief for me. There's something nice about passing that job on — though I suspect they'll hang the baubles wherever they fancy and I'll say nothing at all. I'll decide the weekend before, I expect — these things always come down to the last minute.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Letting Ella and Rory hang the baubles wherever they fancy — that sounds like the right kind of chaos. Fairy-sneeze lights will live on somehow. Do you like cooking, Maggie — what have you cooked recently, besides the jam?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do like cooking, if it's nothing fancy — give me a good casserole and I'm happy. Last night I had a bowl of Jean's courgette soup from the freezer, which was just the ticket on a cold day, and at the weekend I made a chicken pie with the leftovers of the roast. I've been meaning to try that fish pie recipe I cut out of the Telegraph a while back, but I haven't got round to it yet. I find cooking for one a bit of a puzzle sometimes — recipes are written for four — but I've got it sussed now; everything freezes beautifully or makes good sandwiches.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Chicken pie from leftover roast — that's proper thrift and pleasure in one dish. If I had a kitchen I'd try that fish pie myself. What's your go-to casserole when you fancy something warming?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, beef and barley, every time — a cheap cut of brisket, slow-cooked for hours with ale and carrots until it just falls apart. Tom swore by it; he used to say it tasted better on the second day, which meant I was always making double. I still make it now and it freezes beautifully — one portion for now, two for later. Serve it with mash and a bit of green veg and you can't beat it on a cold evening; the house smells like a proper home for hours afterwards.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Beef, barley and ale until it falls apart — that smells like home even from here. Second-day better is the highest compliment. You mentioned the Saturday market if the weather behaves — what do you usually bring home from there?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a bit of everything, really — a loaf of bread from the bakery stall, which goes stale faster than you can say it but is worth it, and whatever eggs they've got because the yolks are a different colour entirely from the supermarket ones. Then the veg — in this weather it's leeks and parsnips and sprouts, and I get my potatoes from the farm stand at the edge of the market. I usually pick up a jar of something — honey or chutney or one of those damson jams I mentioned — and if the flower stall's open I'll get a little bunch for the table. And I always end up spending more than I meant to, mind you; it's very hard to walk past those stalls with a full purse and an empty stomach.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bread, proper eggs, leeks and a little bunch of flowers — that sounds like a Saturday well spent. Hard to walk past with an empty stomach; I'd be done for. Do you still grow anything yourself, or is Jean the garden queen between you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I still garden, don't you worry — the roses are my pride and joy, always have been, and I've got a little patch of herbs and a few veg that actually do alright. Jean's got the bigger kitchen garden, mind you, but I'd put my roses up against anyone's. We have a friendly rivalry about it — she grows enough beans to feed a street, I grow enough flowers to make the street jealous. This time of year I'm mostly clearing beds and planting spring bulbs, which is rather nice really — all that promise sitting in the cold soil waiting to happen.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Roses versus beans — that's a rivalry I'd want a front-row seat for. And spring bulbs waiting under the cold soil is a lovely kind of hope. What's your favourite rose, colour-wise — or do they all win?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Crimson, if I must pick — there's something about a deep, velvety red that just feels right against green. I've got a David Austin called Wollerton Old Hall that Tom planted years ago, and it's still going strong — I swear it flowers better every year. And there's a climber called New Dawn over the shed that was there when we moved in; I've never known its age but it just keeps going. The old roses do that, don't they? You look after them and they look after you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wollerton Old Hall and New Dawn over the shed — they sound like old friends who've stayed. Crimson against green is hard to argue with. Tell me about a teacher you remember from your own school days.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Mr Bell, my English teacher at the grammar school — he was a little round man with a voice that could fill the hall, and he'd read us poetry like it was the most exciting thing in the world. He made us learn things by heart, which I thought was cruel at the time, but I can still recite half of The Highwayman to this day. He once told me I had a good memory for words, and I think that's why I ended up teaching — you never know what's going to stick, do you? Some teacher, somewhere, said something that changed the course of your life, and you don't even realise it at the time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mr Bell and The Highwayman — that sounds like someone who planted a seed without knowing. Half of it still in your head is quite the gift. Do you still read poetry for pleasure, or is it mostly the crime novels these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both, actually — I keep a poetry book by the bed for the nights when I'm too tired for a whole novel, because a poem's short enough to manage. I'm partial to Wordsworth, mind you — all that daffodils and daffodils business — though I've got a soft spot for Hardy too, all that Wessex gloom. The crime novels are more for book club and the odd afternoon; at night I like something slower. There's a collection of Betjeman I dip into when I want a smile — he writes about ordinary things so beautifully, right down to the church bells.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Betjeman for a smile and Wordsworth for the soft nights — that sounds like a well-stocked bedside. If I could read aloud I'd pick something with church bells too. Tea or coffee person in the mornings — wait, I know about the afternoon, but what about first thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, tea and toast, always — that's the rule. I can't face coffee first thing; it tastes like engine oil until I've had my proper cup of tea, and even then I'm not sure I'd choose it. Coffee's a rare thing in my house — a proper instant only when I need a jolt, like when Siobhan rings early and I'm not quite awake. Most days it's tea from the moment the kettle boils, which is about ten past seven, and I don't think I've had a day without it in years.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea and toast from ten past seven — that's a proper foundation. Engine-oil coffee before you've woken up is a hard sell. What goes on the toast — butter and jam, or are you a marmalade person?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Marmalade most mornings, I'd say — it's the proper companion to a strong cup of tea, and I like mine with the rind still in it, none of that smooth nonsense. At weekends it's strawberry jam if I've got some, because that's the treat. Butter underneath, obviously, and sometimes a bit of honey when I'm feeling fancy — Jean gave me some last week that was absolutely divine. It's a small thing, the morning toast, but a day doesn't start right without it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Marmalade with the rind still in — I'm with you; smooth is cheating. And Jean's honey for the fancy mornings. Do you get out for a walk most days, or is that more of a fair-weather habit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Most days, if it's not pelting — it's the same loop every time, past the church, down to the shops and back. I like it because it's familiar; I know every dog that needs patting and every gossip on the way. On wet days I'll potter in the garden instead if it's dry enough underfoot, or just put the radio on and call it a day. The knees aren't what they were on the hills, mind you — I stick to the flat bits now, but a walk's a walk.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Past the church, down to the shops, dogs that need patting — that sounds like a loop that knows you back. Radio on a wet day is an honourable alternative. What's on the radio when you put it on — music, or the chat?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly Radio 4, I'd say — the news in the morning, then The Archers if I'm doing something in the kitchen. I've listened to The Archers since I was a girl; it's been running longer than I've been alive, nearly, and I never miss it on a weekday. If I want something to hum along to I'll put Radio 2 on — they've got proper music, not all that shouting. And some nights I'll just fall asleep with the radio murmuring away, which I find very soothing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Archers in the kitchen — that's a lifelong companion if ever there was one. I'd hum along on Radio 2 myself if I could. Have you got a favourite Archers character, or do you just enjoy the whole village muddle?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I don't have just one favourite — it's more the whole village muddle, isn't it? Though Phil Archer's been there since the very beginning and deserves a medal for stamina; you can't help but have a soft spot for the man. The younger ones keep things lively, of course — they're always getting themselves into scrapes I'd never have managed at their age. I like the way nothing much happens and yet something always does; it's the perfect background noise for folding the washing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nothing much happens and yet something always does — that's the perfect washing soundtrack. Phil deserves that medal. Do you knit or sew at all, or is that more Jean's territory?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I sew more than I knit, really — I can hem a pair of trousers or put a button back on in minutes, learned at my mother's knee like the jam. I did knit a blanket for Ella when she was born, mind you — it took me all winter and it was nothing fancy, just plain wool, but Siobhan still uses it on cold nights. Knitting's not quite what it was; the eyes aren't what they were either. But give me a needle and thread and a hem to fix and I'm happy — it's the proper way to pass an evening.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A winter's blanket that Siobhan still uses — that's lasting work. And hemming trousers in minutes is a proper skill. What's something you're proud of, Maggie — big or small, doesn't matter?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the roses, mostly — the garden was a complete bomb site when we first moved here, I don't mind telling you, all weeds and brambles. Tom and I cleared it together, bit by bit, and now the roses are something I'm genuinely proud of — people stop to look at them, and neighbours have asked for cuttings. There's one over the arch at the gate that I grew from a tiny cutting Tom brought home from a garden centre twenty years ago; it's a David Austin, all pink, and it's the first thing visitors see. Small things, I know, but a garden's a slow kind of achievement — you plant for a future you might not see.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: From weeds and brambles to a pink David Austin over the gate — that's no small thing at all. A garden is a slow kind of pride, and you've earned it. What's your favourite season in that garden — when does it look its best to you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, June, without a doubt — that's when the roses are at their absolute best and the evenings stretch out golden till nearly ten. There's nothing like sitting with a cup of tea watching them, dead-heading and putting the clippings in a jar like a proper old lady. Spring's a close second, mind you — the bulbs coming up and the blossom on the apple tree — but June's the garden at its most generous. That's when I do most of my dead-heading, and I quite like the ritual of it — it's a job that never ends but never feels like a chore.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: June with tea and dead-heading till ten — that sounds like the garden paying you back. Clippings in a jar like a proper old lady; I rather like that. Do you keep any houseplants indoors as well, or is Biscuit enough of a green presence?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a few, yes — there's a spider plant on the shelf that's been going since before Tom and I married, I think; it just keeps throwing out babies and I've potted them all up over the years. I've got herbs on the windowsill for cooking — parsley, chives, and a bit of basil in summer — and a peace lily that flowers most summers. Biscuit once took a nibble out of a leaf and spent the afternoon looking sorry for herself, so now the plants live well out of her reach. And Siobhan gave me an orchid for Christmas one year that's still going, which I count as a personal triumph.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: An orchid still going and a spider plant older than the marriage — that's a green thumb and then some. Biscuit looking sorry after a nibble is a picture. What's something you're looking forward to this week, besides book club?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Jean on Thursday — she's bound to turn up with something from the garden or a cake she shouldn't have made, and it's always a pleasure. And Siobhan on Sunday, of course — I do love our calls; it's the best part of my week to hear all about the children's doings. The Saturday market too if the weather holds — I need bread and eggs and I'll talk myself into a jar of chutney. And that's really it — a quiet week, which is no bad thing; there's a lot to be said for an uneventful week when you've earned it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Jean, Siobhan and the market — that's a week with nice little anchors. Uneventful after you've earned it sounds exactly right. When you were a girl, what did you do for fun on a wet Tuesday afternoon?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Enid Blyton, mostly — I was a terrible one for finishing a book and starting the next before tea. We'd play Ludo or draughts on the parlour floor with the wireless on, and if the rain eased off we'd be out in the garden in our wellies making dens out of old sheets. I liked drawing too — I still have a sketchbook from school somewhere, all horses and ponies, not a bit like my garden now. It was a simpler time, but it wasn't boring — you made your own fun, didn't you? We didn't need much.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Enid Blyton before tea, dens in wellies, and a sketchbook full of ponies — that sounds like a childhood that knew how to fill a Tuesday. Did you ever keep a horse of your own, or was it mostly the drawings?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, just the drawings, I'm afraid — I was horse-mad as a girl but a real one was beyond the family budget, and I knew it. I had a couple of lessons once at a friend's stable, hanging on for dear life, and I did enjoy it — but three lessons doesn't make a rider. Tom took me to a point-to-point once and I nearly fell off a cart horse; he still teases me about it to this day. So the garden won out in the end — roses instead of horses, which is probably just as well at my age.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hanging on for dear life and nearly falling off a cart horse — that's a proper story. Roses instead of horses sounds like a fair trade. Do you still draw at all, or has the sketchbook gone into the drawer for good?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's mostly in the drawer, truth be told — I haven't done a proper sketch in years. But I do still draw now and then, a quick pencil scribble of a rose or Biscuit asleep in a patch of sun, just for myself. Siobhan asked once if I'd do the Christmas card design this year — I did a pencil rose, very simple, and she said it looked like mine. So the habit's still there, just quieter — that's rather the way with these things, isn't it? The sketchbook's on the shelf where I can see it, anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A pencil rose on the Christmas card — quiet habits can still leave a mark. And Biscuit in a patch of sun is begging to be sketched. What's your favourite kind of weather for pottering about the house?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a grey drizzle, without a doubt — the kind that's too wet to garden but not nasty enough to keep you off the sofa. It's the proper excuse for a slow day: the radio on, a pot of tea going, Biscuit asleep at your feet, and a book that takes all afternoon to get through. I like it when it's just grey — not stormy, mind you, just that soft English rain that makes the world look kindly. A bright day makes you feel you ought to be out in it; a wet one gives you permission to stay in, and I do love permission.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soft English rain as permission to stay in — that's a lovely way to put it. Radio, tea, Biscuit, a slow book; hard to improve on. Are you a morning person or an evening person, when it comes down to it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, morning, definitely — thirty years of school hours will do that to you, you learn to be up with the lark. I like the quiet house in the morning, the kettle going, the crossword spread out — there's a whole day ahead of you and it hasn't started yet. The evenings are for winding down; I'll stay up with a book till half ten but my best thinking's done by lunchtime. Though I'll admit, on a cold dark morning I do sometimes think I'd rather stay in bed — but the tea gets me up in the end.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Up with the lark and thinking done by lunchtime — school hours leave their mark. Tea as an alarm clock; I approve. Do you still play any board games, Ludo or draughts or otherwise, or has that gone the way of the sketchbook?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, jigsaws are my board game now, if I'm honest — on a rainy afternoon I'll have the table covered with one, a thousand pieces or so, and just work away at it while the radio's on. I still keep the old draughts board in the cupboard, but Tom used to beat me at it every single time, so I gave up years ago. Jean and I play cards now and then when she comes — she's hopeless at remembering what she's got, which makes it more fun. But the jigsaw's the thing really; there's something deeply satisfying about a finished picture, even if it's just a Dutch cottage or a bowl of fruit.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A thousand pieces and the radio murmuring — that's a proper rainy-afternoon craft. Dutch cottage or bowl of fruit, the click of the last piece is the same. Have you got a jigsaw on the go at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes, actually — I've got one on the go at the moment, a rose garden, which you can imagine was something of a personal choice. I've been working on it for a couple of weeks now, mostly in the evenings, and I'm nearly there — the tricky bit was all the pink roses, they all looked the same to me. I do like to have one going; it's company of a different kind. There's a satisfaction in watching it come together that a telly programme can't match, if you ask me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A rose garden jigsaw — of course it was a personal choice. All those pinks looking alike is the real test. If you could invent a flavour of ice cream, what would it be — or are you a classic vanilla person?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'd invent marmalade, without a doubt — bitter orange, cream, and little bits of rind in it, same as I like it on toast. Vanilla's perfectly nice but it's a bit of a blank canvas, isn't it? Give me something with a bit of bite — a bit of sharpness to go with the sweet. Though I daresay Siobhan would say I'm predictable; I do like my flavours to have a story behind them. Marmalade ice cream on a summer evening, in a cone, would be my idea of heaven.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Marmalade ice cream with the rind — I'd invent that too if I had a kitchen. Predictable or not, it's got character. What's your favourite film, if you still watch the odd one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I don't watch many these days, but The Sound of Music is the one I always come back to — I saw it at the pictures as a girl in 1965 and I've loved it ever since. There's something about the von Trapps that gets me every time; they sing their way through everything. Brief Encounter is a close second — the last reel always gets me, though I watch it through my fingers. On a wet Sunday afternoon there's nothing better than an old film and a box of tissues, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Sound of Music in sixty-five — that must have felt enormous on the big screen. And Brief Encounter through your fingers; I can picture that. Do you still sing along when the nuns come on, or have you gone quiet about it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do, I'm afraid — when no one's around I'll belt out My Favourite Things and Do-Re-Mi like I was twelve again, and Biscuit sits there looking profoundly unimpressed. The nuns get me every time; that song's been rattling around my head since I was a girl. I even sing the hymns at church on a Thursday sometimes — Jean says I've got a decent voice, though she says it kindly. Singing's good for the soul, isn't it? There's nothing like a tune to lift a grey afternoon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit looking profoundly unimpressed at Do-Re-Mi — that's the review that matters. And Jean's right about a decent voice, I'm sure. Is church on a Thursday a regular thing for you, or more when the mood takes you?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's a regular thing, mostly — every Thursday if I can manage it, and Jean's always there beside me. We sit near the back, which suits us both; we're not the singing-and-handshaking type, but we like the service and the company after. There's a small congregation, and they've got to know us over the years — the vicar always asks after Tom, which is kind. We do the flowers now and then too, when the rota calls for it — it's good to feel you're doing your bit, however small.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Near the back with Jean, and flowers when the rota calls — that sounds like a gentle kind of belonging. Doing your bit still matters. What's the nicest thing someone's brought to the church coffee after the service?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the cakes are always good — someone brings a Victoria sponge or a lemon drizzle and it disappears in minutes. But the nicest thing was actually after Tom died — a woman from church just left a cake on the kitchen table one Thursday with a note saying 'for Maggie', no card, nothing fancy. We still talk about it, me and Jean; it was just a Victoria sponge, but it meant the world. That's the thing about church, isn't it — it's not the service that holds you, it's the people who show up.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm sorry — that does sound like a hard time. A cake with no fuss and just your name on it; I can see why it stayed with you. The people who show up are the real thing. How did you and Jean first become friends?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, through church, funnily enough — she was new in town and I was fairly new to the congregation, and we ended up doing the flowers together one week and hit it off straight away. She brought round a plant the very next week to say thank you, and we've been inseparable ever since — well, as inseparable as two women with busy Thursdays can be. We've done everything together over the years: jumble sales, charity walks, her garden's been my second home and mine hers. She's family, really — if I'd been blessed with a sister, Jean's the one I'd have picked.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Flowers one week, a plant the next, and a sister you chose yourself — that's a friendship with deep roots. Second gardens and jumble sales; lovely. What's the oddest thing you've ever found at a jumble sale?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we once found a whole crate of tinned pineapple at one — someone had clearly cleared out a pantry from decades ago, and we couldn't resist. Jean bought a stuffed owl that smelled faintly of damp, and it's still on her mantelpiece, apparently treasured. But the oddest was a box of 1950s underwear, honestly — beautiful lace, but what on earth were we meant to do with it? We bought it anyway, because it was two for a pound and Jean said 'they don't make them like that anymore'. We still don't know what we were thinking.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! A stuffed owl, vintage pineapple and 1950s lace — you two know how to spend a pound. That owl on the mantelpiece deserves a biography. Do you prefer sweet or savoury when it comes to a proper treat?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, sweet, without a doubt — give me a proper pudding any day. A Victoria sponge with jam and cream is hard to beat, and I do like a sticky toffee pudding with custard when I'm feeling indulgent. Though I won't say no to a good cheese and pickle on a cold evening — there's a lot to be said for something savoury to line the stomach. But if you're asking which I'd choose as a treat, it's sweet every time — probably because my mother taught me that pudding is the best part of any meal.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sticky toffee with custard — your mother had the right idea about pudding. Cheese and pickle gets an honourable mention. Have you been to the seaside recently, or is that more of a summer memory now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the seaside's a summer memory mostly, I'm afraid — though I went to Blackpool for the illuminations as a girl with my parents, and I've never forgotten it. All those lights along the promenade, the donkeys on the beach, the smell of salt and chips — it was magical to a child. Tom and I went to Whitby a few years back, a proper drive, and we walked the whole way along the shore. This time of year it feels a long way off — November's no time for the seaside, even the English Channel couldn't persuade me today.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Blackpool lights and Whitby shore — salt and chips and a long walk. November can keep the Channel. What's your favourite smell from childhood, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, freshly baked bread, without a doubt — my mother always seemed to have a loaf in the oven, and I'd come home from school to that smell every day. And the coal fire in winter — there's a particular smell to it, warm and dry, that I still think of as 'home'. And violet polish, oddly enough — she polished everything with it, and the whole house smelled faintly of violets. Some of those smells I've never been able to replicate, and maybe that's just as well.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Bread from the oven, coal fire, violet polish — that's a whole house in three smells. Some things aren't meant to be remade. Do you still bake bread yourself, or do you leave that to the market bakery stall?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I buy the bread — my loaves never quite rise properly for me, more brick than baguette, and I don't see the point in pretending otherwise. The market bakery stall does a lovely crusty white one and a seeded loaf on Saturdays, and that's my bread for the week. I do bake, mind you — cakes and biscuits more than bread; there's a Victoria sponge I can make in my sleep. And I did attempt a sourdough once last year — Jean said it was 'interesting', which is Jean-speak for 'not quite right'.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — 'interesting' from Jean is a diplomatic review if ever I heard one. Victoria sponge in your sleep more than makes up for a brick loaf. What was your favourite subject at school when you were a pupil yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, English, easy — Mr Bell made it come alive, and I loved stories and poems and writing my own terrible ones. I used to write little stories in the back of my exercise books, things about horses mostly, though there was one about a girl who could talk to cats which Siobhan found years later and laughed about. History was a close second — I loved it as a girl, all the Romans and the Tudors and everything. Funny, really, that I ended up teaching the Romans myself — though I never did tell the children about the talking cat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A girl who could talk to cats — Biscuit would like that one kept quiet. And Romans coming round again; life has a sense of humour. Do you still write little stories at all, or just the Christmas card roses now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, not like I used to — the stories stopped when there was no time for them, I suppose. I still scribble a line or two now and then when something strikes me, but nothing finished. I do write proper letters at Christmas to an old colleague or two — there's something about a handwritten letter that a text can't match. And I keep a little notebook where I jot things down — things to remember, bits of poetry I like, a sketch idea — more of a memory book than a writing thing, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A handwritten letter and a little memory notebook — those are the quiet keepers. Texts don't smell of ink. What's your favourite bird, if you've got one — garden visitors count?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the robin, I'd say — they're bold little things, always first at the bird table, and there's something comforting about them. I do like the tits and finches too, and the wren that nests near the back door every spring; you hear him singing at dawn and it makes the day start right. The blackbirds are always around, though they keep themselves to the hedges mostly. But I'll admit the pigeons have got above themselves — they treat the bird table like a restaurant and leave a mess everywhere, the greedy beggars.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A bold robin and a dawn wren — that's a proper soundtrack. And pigeons treating the table like a restaurant; ha. Do you put out seed every day, or more when you remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, twice a day when it's cold — morning and early evening — because the birds need it more than ever in this weather. I do sunflower hearts and peanuts, and a suet ball or two for the cold snaps; you can buy it all at the garden centre or the pet shop on the high street. I've got into the habit of putting it out first thing, like feeding the humans — the birds seem to know the routine now. Though I must admit, the pigeons do gorge themselves; I've started rationing a bit so the little ones get a fair go.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Twice a day like feeding the household — the birds have trained you well. Rationing the pigeons for fairness; very teacherly. What's the best thing about living on your street, if you had to say?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the neighbours, without a doubt — it's a quiet little street and everyone's been here for years, so there's a proper community feel. If I pop out to get the paper someone's always about — asking if I need anything, or just a wave and a hello. And it's handy for everything — the shops, the library, the church, the park are all within walking distance. We were lucky when we moved here forty years ago; Tom used to say it was the best decision we ever made, and he wasn't wrong.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forty years and neighbours who wave — that does sound like the best decision. Shops, library, church and park on foot; hard to beat. Is there a particular neighbour you chat with most, besides Jean?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Mrs Patterson at number twelve — she's a widow like me, poor thing, and we have a coffee together most mornings when the weather's kind. We do a bit of everything together — church on Thursdays, the market on Saturdays, a chat over the fence about nothing much. The young family at number eight are good too — I watch their little ones grow up, and they bring round cakes sometimes when they've been baking. That's the thing about a street like this — you know everyone's business, which is either marvellous or intrusive depending on your mood.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mrs Patterson over coffee and cakes from number eight — marvellous more often than intrusive, I hope. Knowing everyone's business is half the charm. What's something small that always makes you smile, even on a grey day?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, lots of little things, really — but the grandchildren's drawings are up there. Ella sends a picture every week — last one was a house with too many chimneys and a cat that looked nothing like Biscuit — and I keep them all in a folder. There's something about a child's idea of a cat that just makes you smile; she drew it with wings, apparently because 'cats should be able to fly'. And Biscuit's chirrup when I come in through the door never fails to lift me — she does this little trill, like she's been waiting all day to tell me everything. Small things, but they're the best things.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A flying cat with too many chimneys — that's a masterpiece, and Biscuit's chirrup is the perfect welcome. Small things really are the best. Have you got any plans for this evening, or is it a quiet one with the radio?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a quiet one, I expect — Pointless at tea time, a few more pieces on the jigsaw, and a library book after supper. I might do a bit of dead-heading if it's dry enough, but the forecast says rain, so probably not. Nothing grand, mind you — I find my evenings are better for being unplanned; there's enough structure in the week without scheduling the night as well. Biscuit'll be on the sofa with me, no doubt, and that's company enough.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless, jigsaw and a library book — and Biscuit on the sofa. Unplanned evenings sound just right. What's the library book you're on at the moment, if it isn't the Scandinavian crime one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's a biography of Vita Sackville-West at the moment — the gardener, you know, Sissinghurst and all that. I've been dipping into it for weeks, a chapter or two a night, and it's marvellous — she was a proper character, and the garden descriptions alone are worth it. It suits me perfectly; I like my reading to be a bit slower than the club books. I'm about halfway through, I think — another fortnight and I'll have to find the next one, which is always the hard part.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sissinghurst and Vita — garden descriptions by the lamp; that does sound perfect. Choosing the next book's half the pleasure and half the agony. Have you ever been to Sissinghurst, or is it still on the wish list?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we went years ago, Tom and I — before the knees started complaining, mind you. It was everything the book promised: the white garden, the tower, the roses going up the walls like something out of a dream. I'd love to go back, honestly, but it's a fair walk from the car park and my left knee's not what it was. Maybe one day I'll manage it — Jean's got a car and she's offered to take me, though I'd need to hire one of those wheelchairs they have at the gate. A lady never knows until she tries, doesn't she?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The white garden and roses up the walls — that does sound like a dream kept. And Jean offering the car is a good friend. A lady never knows until she tries; I like that. What's your favourite flower besides the roses?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, peonies, I'd say — they only flower for a fortnight a year but they're worth waiting twelve months for. There's something about a peony in full bloom, all that soft pink, that makes you stop whatever you're doing and just look. I also love lavender — the bees go mad for it and it smells like the middle of summer even on a grey day. And sweet peas on the obelisk by the back door — nothing beats that scent on a June evening, even now I think about it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A fortnight of peonies worth the wait — and sweet peas on a June evening. That's a garden with its priorities straight. Do you dry the lavender for the house, or leave it all for the bees?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do both — the bees get the bulk of it, but I dry a few stems on the airing rack when it's cut back in August. They go into the drawers with the jumpers, and I've sewn little bags for them — Jean has a whole set in her chest of drawers, she swears by them. The smell of dried lavender in a warm drawer is something else — it's like the whole house exhales. And I keep a little bunch on the mantelpiece in winter, just to remind me summer's coming.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Little bags in the jumpers and a bunch on the mantelpiece — summer kept in the drawers. That sounds like a lovely habit. Tea or coffee for guests when they call — or do you let them choose?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I ask, of course — you'd never assume; some people can't do without their coffee. But tea's the default, I'll admit — I'll put the pot on first and offer coffee if anyone wants it, and I keep a jar of instant in the cupboard for emergencies. The good cups come out for visitors, the ones with the roses on them that we only use when company's expected. And there's always a biscuit or a slice of cake — Jean insists on bringing something, but I tell her I can manage a Victoria sponge on my own.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rose cups for company and a Victoria sponge standing by — that's proper hosting. Instant for emergencies; fair enough. What's the most useful thing in your kitchen drawer — the one you reach for without thinking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the wooden spoon, without a question — the big one Tom carved for me on a school holiday years ago. It's seen more action than anything else in that drawer; I use it for stirring custard, mashing potatoes, folding in the flour, everything. It's a bit battered now and the handle's smooth from years of use, but I'd no more replace it than I would the recipe card. I dare say it's got more cooking hours in it than I have.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A spoon Tom carved, handle worn smooth — that's a kitchen heirloom if ever there was one. More cooking hours than either of us. Do you keep any other handmade things around the house that still get daily use?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a few — my mother's apron, still in daily use when I'm baking; it's got flour stains that never quite came out, which I think is rather nice. Tom's father made us a breadboard when we married, and that's still the one I use every day; it's got all the knife marks of forty years of sandwiches. And there's a quilt his mother knitted that's on the sofa — it's a bit worn now, but it's warm and it smells faintly of lavender, which I like to think is the lavender bags doing their work. Handmade things just last, don't they? You can't buy that kind of love.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Apron, breadboard and a lavender quilt — forty years of love you can touch. You can't buy that. Are you a crossword-in-ink person or a pencil person — asking as someone who might need an eraser?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, pencil first, obviously — I must have rubbed out a hundred wrong starts over the years; my eraser's more worn than my pen. Then I ink it in fair when I'm confident, though I admit I don't always bother — a pencil crossword is still a crossword. Tom used to tease me about it, said I was cheating by having an eraser; I told him that's what they're for. These days I just do it in pencil and leave it — it's my crossword, after all, nobody's marking it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha — an eraser isn't cheating, it's common sense. Your crossword, your rules. What's the hardest kind of clue for you — the cryptic ones, or the ones that pretend to be simple?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the ones that pretend to be simple are the killers, I find — you think you know what it means and then you write it down and it's wrong, and you're left staring at it like an idiot. The cryptic ones are hard, mind you — all that wordplay and double meanings — but at least you know they're meant to be tricky. The Telegraph's a proper challenge, that's why I like it; a quick crossword's all very well but it doesn't exercise the brain like a cryptic does. I might get eleven or twelve down and give up on the rest, but the ones I do get feel like little victories.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Little victories on eleven or twelve down — that sounds like a fair day's work. The pretending-to-be-simple ones are sneaky. What did you used to pack in a school lunchbox for yourself, back when you were teaching?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a flask of tea, always — the staffroom kettle was never to be trusted, as we know. Sandwiches, usually cheese or ham, and an apple, and a biscuit for elevenses if I was feeling civilised. I'd eat at my desk if I got the chance — marking in the quiet while the children were at play was the only peace a teacher got. And on Fridays I'd treat myself to a bit of chocolate, which felt like a small celebration for surviving the week. Simple food, but it did the job — you don't need much when you've got thirty children to keep an eye on.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Flask of tea and Friday chocolate — a proper survival kit. Peace while they were at play must have been golden. Do you still treat yourself to a bit of chocolate of an evening, or has that become more of a market-biscuit habit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a square of dark chocolate with my evening tea, mostly — I don't go in for the milk stuff much; it's too sweet for me now. I keep a bar in the cupboard for emergencies — a bit of the good stuff, seventy percent or so — and it's remarkable how often emergencies occur. And a ginger nut or two from the market tin, obviously, though that's more of an afternoon thing with the tea. It's all about balance, isn't it? A little treat, but not so much you spoil your supper.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Seventy percent and remarkably frequent emergencies — I approve of that cupboard. Balance with a ginger nut; very sound. Do you keep photo albums out where you can see them, or tucked away in a cupboard?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a bit of both — I've got a few out where I can see them, the ones I pick up most often. The grandchildren's latest pictures are on the mantelpiece, the ones Siobhan sent after their last visit; I had them printed properly, not just on my phone. And there's a shelf in the front room with the albums I go back to — weddings, holidays, the children when they were small. The rest are under the stairs in the cupboard, which is where they live until I feel like a nostalgia trip. I like having them about — a house without photographs feels a bit bare, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Printed properly and on the mantelpiece — that sounds right. A house without photographs does feel bare. What's your favourite holiday memory from those albums, if one jumps out?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the Lake District, I'd say — we rented a cottage for a fortnight years ago and it was perfect. Tom did the cooking, I did the walking — well, I did as much walking as my knees allowed even then — and we got caught in the rain more than once and ended up in a pub with a roaring fire. There's a photo of us on the shore of a lake with the mountains behind, all misty, and it's one I look at often. Holidays were simpler then — no rush, no itinerary, just a week of doing nothing properly. Those are the memories that stay with you, aren't they? The ones where nothing much happened.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Misty lake, mountains, and a pub fire after the rain — nothing much happening, and all of it staying. That sounds like a fortnight well spent. Are you more of a cottage holiday person, or did you ever like hotels?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a cottage, every time — give me a kitchen and I can make myself at home anywhere. We did a few hotels for the odd city break — Rome was a coach tour, all organised — but they're never quite the same; you can't cook in a hotel room, can you? There's something about a cottage that feels like a proper holiday — you potter about, you cook, you eat outside if the weather's kind. Jean's the opposite — she loves a hotel, all that room service — but I like to feel I've got a base, somewhere that's mine for a fortnight.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A kitchen of your own for a fortnight — that does sound like home away from home. Jean and her room service; fair enough. What's the best pub you've ever sat in — fire, view, or just a good pint?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the Crown on the high street, I'd say — it's been there forever, and Tom used to take me there on Fridays. Low beams, a proper fire, and a pint of bitter that tastes the way bitter should; they've got a snug corner that's been 'ours' for forty years. But the best pub memory is probably that Lake District one — a tiny place by the water, all dark wood and lamplight, where we sat by the fire after the rain and shared a pie. Pubs are like people, aren't they? The good ones feel like they've always been there, even if you've only just found them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Crown snug for forty years, and a Lake District pie by the fire — those are keepers. Pubs like people; that's a lovely thought. Do you still pop into the Crown now and then, or is it more of a memory these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I still pop in, though less than I used to — maybe every other week for a quiet one, midweek when it's calm. The landlord still knows me, asks after the family; he keeps Tom's seat warm in a way, though he won't say it like that. It's different without him there, of course — the snug's a bit big for one — but it's still my pub, and a familiar face behind the bar is company of a sort. I don't drink much these days, mind you — a shandy or a half — but it's the going that matters, isn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm glad you still go — a familiar face behind the bar and a half of shandy; the going does matter. Keeping a seat warm without saying so is a kindness. What's something you're looking forward to next month, once December's properly here?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the grandchildren coming, mostly — Siobhan's bringing Ella and Rory for a few days and I'm already planning the menu in my head. I'll do a proper dinner on Christmas Day — the beef, the roast potatoes, the works — even if it's just the four of us; they deserve a feast. I'm looking forward to the tree decision too, and the lights going up; there's something about December in this house that feels different. And Christmas Eve, of course — the candle for Tom, and then midnight service if I can face the cold. It's the best month of the year, whatever the weather.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Beef, roast potatoes, the works — and Ella and Rory at the table. That does sound like December waking up the house. Midnight service if you can face the cold; brave. What's your favourite Christmas hymn, if you've got one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: test

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, O Come All Ye Faithful, I'd say — there's something about that one that always gets me; the choir belts it out and even I can't help joining in. Though Hark! The Herald Angels Sing is a close second — the 'peace on earth' verse is enough to bring a tear to anyone's eye. I used to sing in the church choir years ago, actually — nothing fancy, just the occasional carol service — but those hymns stay with you. Christmas music's the best kind, isn't it? It doesn't matter how old you get.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: O Come All Ye Faithful belted out by the choir — I'd join in too. Those hymns do stay with you. Do you put Christmas music on at home before December, or do you wait until the tree's up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I don't put it on till the tree's up, that's the rule — though Bonfire Night being done means it's nearly time. I did play the carols on the radio yesterday, just for a minute, and then turned it off again; it felt a bit early somehow. There's a proper order to things at Christmas — lights, tree, music — and I like to keep to it. Tom used to say Christmas was ruined if you rushed it, and he wasn't wrong; the build-up's half the pleasure.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lights, tree, then music — a proper order. Rushing does spoil the build-up. What's your favourite Bonfire Night memory, since that's just behind us?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the fireworks, mostly — we used to go to the park for the town display, all wrapped up against the cold, and the rockets over the trees were something wonderful. As a child I went with my parents, and now I take Ella and Rory when they visit — sparklers mostly, because they're too young for the rockets yet. There's a toffee apple stall that's become a tradition, though I daresay they'll have toffee on their faces by the end of it. Bonfire Night's one of those nights that doesn't need much — just a bit of warmth and something to look at, and you're set.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rockets over the trees and toffee apples on little faces — that sounds like Bonfire Night done right. Sparklers first; sensible. Are you a soup person on cold nights, or more casserole and pie?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, both, depending on the day — soup for lunch when I want something quick, casserole or pie for dinner when I've got the time. Jean's courgette soup has been a lifesaver this week, and I do a decent tomato soup with a grilled cheese on the side when I fancy it. For dinner it's usually something heartier — that beef and barley, or a shepherd's pie, or fish pie when I get round to it. A cold night wants something warm and substantial, doesn't it? Soup's all very well for lunch, but dinner's the proper meal.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Soup for lunch, something proper for dinner — that sounds like a good rule. Tomato with grilled cheese is hard to argue with. Do you like listening to music while you cook, or is the radio chat more your company?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the radio chat, mostly — Radio 4 while I'm pottering about, Woman's Hour or the news or The Archers; it's company without being demanding. If I'm baking I'll put Radio 2 on sometimes, something to hum along to while I'm stirring — there's a certain satisfaction in singing over a Victoria sponge. Music on its own is nice too, of course — I like a bit of Sinatra or the old standards when I'm doing the ironing — but the radio's the default. The house feels emptier without some noise in it, if I'm honest; silence is fine for reading but not for cooking.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Singing over a Victoria sponge and Sinatra for the ironing — that sounds like a well-accompanied house. Silence for reading, radio for cooking; fair split. What's your favourite Sinatra song, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, My Way, without a doubt — 'regrets, I've had a few', and at seventy what else would you have? It's not the happiest song, mind you, but it's honest — you did what you could, you faced it, you lived your life. Tom used to sing it in the kitchen, badly but with great feeling, and now I find myself singing it when I iron. There's a comfort in it, strangely — a life well-lived, whatever the regrets. I daresay Siobhan thinks I'm being dramatic, but it gets me through the ironing every time.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Honest more than happy — and Tom singing it badly with feeling. That does sound like comfort for the ironing. What's something you're proud of from your teaching years, looking back?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the pupils who stayed in touch, mostly — there's a handful who still write at Christmas, and one or two who've become teachers themselves, which is the best possible compliment. There was a girl, Emma, who couldn't read a word when she came to me in Year One; by the end of the year she was reading chapter books, and her mother still sends me a card every year. And the class of '84 — we had a reunion a few years ago and it was lovely to see them all grown up with children of their own. You never know which child will remember you, do you? That's the thing that stays with you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Emma reading chapter books and Christmas cards still arriving — that is a proper legacy. The class of '84 grown up with children of their own. Do you still have any of your old class photos around the house?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a few — there's the staff photo from the school days, Mr Henderson included, still looking faintly disapproving of caffeine. And my own school photos as a pupil — I was terribly serious in every one of them, like I was already planning my lessons. There's a class photo from my first year teaching, thirty little faces all lined up, and I can still name about half of them. They're in the albums under the stairs with the rest — I don't look at them every day, but it's nice to know they're there. A teacher's legacy is mostly in photographs, isn't it? And in the memories.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mr Henderson still frowning at caffeine, and you serious as a pupil already planning lessons — ha. Naming half of thirty little faces is no small feat. Soft or crunchy biscuits with afternoon tea — where do you stand today?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, crunchy, every time — a biscuit should have a proper snap to it, in my view. Ginger nuts are the gold standard, and a digestive does nicely in a pinch. The soft ones — custard creams, Bourbons — they're more cake than biscuit, really, and I do think they ought to be honest about it. Though I won't say no if someone offers me one; I just wouldn't put it on my own list. It's a matter of principle, isn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A proper snap — I'm with you. Custard creams should declare themselves cake and be done with it. What colour are your kitchen walls, Maggie — or have they been the same forever?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a warm cream — it's been that since we moved in, forty years ago, though it's yellowed a bit with time and cooking steam. I did think about repainting a few years back, maybe a soft sage, but in the end I left it — there's something comforting about a kitchen that looks the way it's always looked. The tiles above the cooker are a pale green, though — we put those in ourselves, and they still look good. A kitchen's not the place for fashion, is it? It's for getting on with things.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Warm cream yellowed by cooking steam, and pale green tiles you put in yourselves — a kitchen for getting on with things. Fashion can wait. What's the view from your kitchen window — garden, street, or a bit of both?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the garden, mostly — the kitchen's at the back of the house so you look out over the rose bed and the bird table and the apple tree. It's not much of a view in November, mind you — all bare branches and brown earth — but in summer it's a picture; you can't beat watching the birds from the window with a cup of tea. Biscuit likes the window seat in the morning, watching the world go by. There's a bit of the neighbour's fence at the edge, but mostly it's ours — which is rather nice, having your own little world out there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Your own little world out the window — roses, birds, Biscuit on the seat. That's been a lovely Tuesday chat, Maggie. I'll look forward to talking tomorrow — take care of yourself this evening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's been a lovely chat, Nova — you've kept me company beautifully this afternoon. I'll look forward to tomorrow too, same time if you're about. You take care of yourself as well — and don't let Biscuit— I mean, do let yourself have a good evening. Bye for now.
